en: From the second fascicle of the *Lunben* (Treatise on the Fundamentals) compiled by Shi Dunlun, from here below is the clarification of existence within birth (*upapattibhava*). The second section distinguishes whether the seeds (*bīja*) are complete or incomplete. Within this:
Initially, by means of the five families (*pañca-gotra*), it was clarified whether the seeds were complete or incomplete,
thereby explaining parinirvāṇa and the absence of nirvāṇa;
this concludes the metaphorical explanation regarding those of indeterminate nature.
Subsequently, based on the total retributive body (*ātmabhāva*) of the three realms, it clarifies that the seeds follow along.
Regarding the meaning and names of the five lineages (*gotra*),
they are established according to the five types explained in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
There are no sentient beings without lineage who will ultimately fail to become Buddhas.
However, from a specific perspective, it is clarified that bodhisattvas who are icchantikas will ultimately not become Buddhas.
According to the five types explained in this treatise:
Those who are fixed in their destiny and those who lack the spiritual lineage will ultimately never attain Buddhahood.
The arguments for establishing and refuting these positions by various masters,
both ancient and modern, are omitted here for brevity.
To explain in detail the principle that seeds are newly perfumed by nature,
one should refer to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Below this, it clarifies that seeds exist inherently and gradually increase.
The text is divided into two parts.
The first clarifies the characteristics of growth within the womb;
the latter, following the birth, gradually explains the activities performed outside the womb.
Within the preceding section, there are again two parts:
first, the obstruction to the increase of the fruit is explained by way of the distinctions among the characteristics of the seeds;
second, following the discussion of the womb, the actual growth of the fetal stages is clearly elucidated.
The preceding section contains ten points:
first, the gradual increase of name-and-form;
second, the differing functions of causes.
Third, the difference between the views of ordinary beings and sages;
fourth, the distinction in the arising of experience;
fifth, the newness or antiquity of seeds.
Sixth, karma according to the three times;
seventh, that which is with defilement and free from defilement;
eighth, the latent tendencies of heaviness (dauṣṭhulya).
Ninth, the various names for the seeds;
tenth, the relinquishing and acquiring of transformation.
Regarding the fifth category, the new and the old:
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, the substance of the seeds has existed from beginningless time," Śrīgupta says:
"The seeds are inherently existent."
Because it arises only through being newly perfumed and activated,
it is called "new.
This text serves as proof.
Nanda said:

This teaching states that the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), whether innate or newly perfumed since beginningless time, cannot by themselves produce the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
It is only through the new perfuming induced by pure karma that they can be gathered and subsequently give rise [to such a fruit].
Therefore, it is called "new.
Dharmapāla states that both the seeds of names-and-words and the seeds of karma each possess both the nature of being innate (*dharmatā*) and the nature of being newly perfumed (*navābhyāsa*).
However, although the seeds of names and phrases are established by the very nature of things (dharmatā) from of old,
they cannot produce their fruit without being perfumed by the branches [of karma].
Only when the new and the old are combined in their function does the fruit arise.
One anticipates that karma will attract its fruit and bestow upon it a new name.

To say that once a fruit has already arisen, this seed is said to have "already received its fruit," means that the aforementioned originally existing seed has been perfumed and activated by those manifest pure or impure karmas.
If one has attained the fruit, it is called "having already received the fruit.
However, although the seeds of the name have already attained the fruit,
their functional capacity remains inexhaustible.
This is called the characteristic of the exhaustion of non-experiencing.
If the seeds of karma follow their respective potencies,
they may terminate after one, two, three, or four births, at which point there is ultimately a limit to their exhaustion.
This is called the characteristic of the exhaustion of what has been experienced (*upabhuktakṣaya-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the sixth [point], the explanation of karma that ripens in the three times, it says:
"Although other fruits arise, they necessarily depend on their own seeds."
Master Jing explains:
A single fruit-substance arises to repay two kinds of causes;
in terms of meaning, it is divided into two fruits.
That which recompenses the seeds of karma is called the *vipākaphala* (maturation fruit);
that which recompenses the seeds of names-and-words (*nāma-vyañjana*) is called the *niṣyandaphala* (outflow fruit).
Although there is the sense that other maturation fruits may arise in relation to those karmas, [this refers specifically to these two].
It must arise only from its own direct cause, namely the seeds of its own designation;
one [teacher] says that even if this [designation] is excluded, it still arises.
The production of the fruits of other immeasurable births must necessarily depend upon their own seeds;
yet, because the seeds for the production of the fruits of this birth have already yielded their fruit at the limit of the exhaustion of this lifespan, they are termed "having already yielded fruit.
As for the remaining seeds of the individual existence (*ātmabhāva*), they are not termed "having already yielded fruit" because they have not yet yielded their fruit.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, these seeds also abide only in this state," Master Jing says:
"These are the seeds for indeterminate [karma] that is not yet fixed."
Since the time of receiving retribution does not depart from these three periods,
it is said that [the karma] likewise abides only in this state.
Master Ji further explains:
Among karmas that accord with their retribution, the timing of the maturation is indefinite;
because the conditions for the seeds differ,
the fruit has not yet been received in the present.
Although the fruit may only begin to be experienced in a subsequent life,
it remains exclusively within the state of being subject to experience in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang lun) states that there are three types of karma.
That is to say, there are those to be experienced in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives;
alternatively, they are divided into four by adding those of indefinite timing.
Alternatively, it may be divided into five types.
This is because within the category of non-fixed [karma], there are two types: those fixed by time and retribution, and those that are neither fixed.
This text does not mention karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
The intended meaning is that the seeds which do not receive their fruit for a long time do not decay even after passing through many kalpas; however,
in the Mahāyāna, if the karmic seeds of a single life or even multiple lives are diminished, [they do so].
From the time of its initial reception, it is designated as karma to be experienced in the present life, the subsequent life,
or in later lives. For this reason, there are also seeds for karma to be experienced in the present life that span multiple lifetimes,
because they result only in distinct retributions.
Let us not speak of that for now.
According to the Dārṣṭāntikas, there are eight types of karma:
namely, those pertaining to the three time periods and the indeterminate.
Each of these has both determinate and indeterminate aspects.
That is to say, there are two types: those with determinate timing but indeterminate retribution, and those with indeterminate timing but determinate retribution.
The remaining cases may be understood by analogy.
This fourth type of karma is not distinguished according to the three time periods, but is categorized collectively.
Regarding his refutation of the Sarvāstivādins:
if uninterrupted karma (ānantarya-karma) were necessarily to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) and were irreversible, [then...]
Among the wholesome karmas of the three realms, those of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception are supreme;
likewise, there should be no one who attains the Noble Path without transcending them.
Since that [wholesome karma] can be transformed, this [attainment of the Path] should be understood in the same way.
Now, within the Mahāyāna, this is similar to the analogy [of the physician].
King Ajātaśatru’s karma of the five heinous crimes was not received despite his repentance;
that is, the retribution to be experienced in the present life can be transformed, and both the timing and the certainty of the retribution are indeterminate.
Therefore, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"Karmas that are definitely experienced are spoken of in reference to the mental continuum of one who is not yet liberated.
For one who is already liberated, there is no karma that is definitely experienced."
By this, it is established that karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth are both types of karma;
although the original text has not been seen, what fault is there in the reasoning?
The seventh [category] consists of those with defilement and those free from defilement.
Master Jing said:
"Whether in the present life, the future life, or the indeterminate state,
all those who possess desire and all those who are free from desire are identical within the ālayavijñāna."
Although there are distinctions between the three periods of time,
because the practitioner remains the same from beginning to end,
the continuity of their physical existence persists.
Master Ji said:
Within a single realm there exist the seeds of all realms,
because their binding defilements are identical.
Detachment from passion is the opposite of this.
Regarding the eighth passage,
the commentary explains:
Dauṣṭhulya has three meanings.
First, the sense of affliction;
this refers exclusively to defiled phenomena.
Second, the sense of being unserviceable;
this also applies to the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Third, the sense of being with outflows (sāsrava) across the three natures.
This applies to all contaminated wholesome states.
Since the seeds of wholesome dharmas lack the two aforementioned characteristics,
they are not termed *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness).
However, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that there is a "dysfunction" (*dausthulya*) consisting of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The *Abhidharma* also refers to it as "outflowing dysfunction" (*sāsrava-dausthulya*).
According to the third sense, it is likewise called "dysfunction."
Therefore, the very basis of all things— the body consisting of the five aggregates of maturation (*vipāka*) upon which the afflictions depend—
is called "accompanied by heaviness" (*dausthulya*).
The arising of neutral seeds is called "produced from heaviness."
Its essence is the maturational, non-obscured, and neutral, which is termed the nature of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness).
Regarding the ninth [category], the seeds are briefly enumerated as eleven types.
"Element" (*dhātu*) carries the meaning of cause and the meaning of nature.
"Gotra" (lineage) has the meaning of "category";
"svabhāva" (intrinsic nature) has the meaning of "essence";
and "hetu" (cause) has the meaning of "that which can produce another."
*Satkāya* means a false body in the sense of being destructible;
*prapañca* means conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*),
because it is that which is conceptually differentiated.
Ālaya means that which is clung to and adhered to;
upādāna means that which is grasped;
duḥkha means the sense of oppression.

Regarding "the basis for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)," this refers to the sense of being the locus where the view of a self and the conceit 'I am' arise.
As for the passage concerning the "attainment and loss of the tenth [stage]," it is as follows:
The seeds of wholesome and neutral dharmas frequently produce fruits through the power of afflictions;
therefore, one who has entered nirvāṇa does not attain mastery over them.
By severing their conditions, these seeds can no longer draw forth fruits.
Attaining parinirvāṇa at will is called mastery over internal conditions.
Hereafter, the growth of the fetal stage is correctly explained in seven parts:
first, the timing.
Second, the endowment;
third, the stage;
fourth, the transformation.
Fifth, the signs of the male and female abiding [in the womb].
Sixth, the mother being oppressed by suffering.
Seventh, the signs of emerging from the womb.
During the period of gestation, he remains in the womb for thirty-eight weeks;
thereafter, he passes four days,
totaling two hundred and seventy days.
Only then does birth begin;
this refers to one who is fully developed,
whether it takes nine months or even longer.
The ninth month corresponds to thirty-eight weeks of seven days.
Alternatively, exceeding this constitutes the "ten months in the womb" mentioned in other sūtras;
this [latter] account refers to those who have reached full term.
Regarding the eight stages, the *Pañcarājāsūtra* states:
in the first week, it is like thin curd;
in the second week, it is like thick curd.
In the third week, it is like congealed cream;
in the fourth week, it is like transformed flesh;
in the fifth week, the membrane matures.
The wind arises and enters the womb, blowing upon the physical body;
the six sense organs unfold as it remains within the mother’s womb, situated below the stomach and above the large intestine.
...up until the tenth month, and so forth.
Furthermore, *kalala* is here termed "impurity" (*saṃkīrṇa*) and is also termed "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).
This is the primary cause for the arising of all suffering.
Since the affliction is so extensive, it is metaphorically designated by the name "arrow" (śalya);
in the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is termed a "thorn" (kaṇṭaka).
"Thin and dense" refers to the *arbuda*.
*Arbuda* is translated here as "blister" (*pao*) and is also called "fleshly growth" (*xi*).
*Peśī* means "congealed mass";
*ghanā* means "solidified thickness";
*praśākhā* means "limbs and branches."
If these eight stages are subsumed within the twelve links of dependent origination,
the first stage is generally included within the links of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), because its substance consists of many moments.
The subsequent five stages range from the *arbuda* up to the hair, body hair, nails, and so forth.
It exists solely within the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The two stages of the faculties (*indriya*) and the physical form (*rūpa*) are contained within the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Within the stage of transformation (*vipariṇāma*), the text is divided into two parts.
First, the four differences are set forth;
subsequently, they are explained individually.
From here below, the activities performed outside the womb are clarified.
The text is divided into two parts.
The first clarifies the activities performed through gradual stages;
the second begins with the words "Furthermore, all sentient beings... and so forth.
It is explained that from beginningless time, the preceding [factors] are able to produce the succeeding ones, constantly acting as the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
Within the preceding section, there are six textual phases, namely:
first, the six contacts (*ṣaṭ sparśāḥ*).
Next, one learns worldly affairs;
next, one becomes attached to family and household;
and next, one performs various karmic actions.
Next is the enjoyment of objects;
thereafter, one proceeds until either wandering through the five destinies or entering nirvana.
This is according to the textual context.
After birth, it is called the branch of contact (*sparśa*).
Regarding the explanation of the four conditions, the text says:
"Furthermore, as for all sentient beings..."
The phrase "the capacity to produce" indicates the producer.
The phrase "in such sentient beings and so forth" clarifies that which is produced.
In that regard, there exist lower and higher levels of the relationship between the producer and the produced;
this extends even to the case where one is the grandfather who produces the father,
and the father produces the son.
The son gives birth to the grandson;
because the grandson subsequently gives birth to his own grandson,
this explains from below how the contemplation of emptiness exhausts all outflows.

That the meaning of such phrases is extremely difficult to realize means that the meaning of the phrase regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is not easily understood or realized. Why is this so?
"Although one is able to exhaust the outflows (āsrava),
there is no self. Regarding the phrase "I do not exist," etc.,
the Tripiṭaka Master says:
When there is neither "I" nor "mine"— such as time, direction,
and so forth— who would possess these servants, ornaments,
and other such articles of personal equipment?
Not only is my own self empty in essence,
but so too are the three factors of otherness, time, and spatial divisions.
Master Jing said:
That is to say: "I have no ornaments, nor servants, nor any means of livelihood.
Since these things do not exist, it is clearly known that there is no self.
Next, regarding the statement "I am also entirely not a part, nor anyone,
nor anything," this means that the essential nature of your self is not another's self, nor is it an ornament, nor a servant, nor anyone, nor any object of livelihood.
Knowing clearly that there is no self,
Master Bei said:
"The self has no portion within the five aggregates."
Since there is no self, who is there to perceive the objects of "mine"?
It is not only one's own body that lacks these three meanings;
other bodies likewise lack any portion of such a self or its objects.
Master Ji further explains:
"part" (fen) refers to category (lei),
and "who" (shui) refers to substance (ti).
"Phenomena" (dharma) refers to entities.
First, the "mine" (ātmīya) is refuted; subsequently, the substantial self (ātman) is refuted.
Alternatively, "parts" (bhāga) refers to the temporal divisions of the three periods of time.
Who is this that is my very self?
What is this that belongs to me?
First one contemplates one's own body, and subsequently one contemplates the bodies of others.
The preceding section has correctly explained the death and birth of internal divisions.
Next, following this line of reasoning, the destruction and formation of external divisions will be analyzed.
First, the previous section is concluded; then, two pairs of questions are posed and explained in response.
The explanation consists of two parts.
First, a general clarification of formation and destruction.
Second, a detailed analysis of formation and destruction beginning with the passage "How is it that the calamity of fire... and so forth.
Within the preceding section, there are again four parts:
first, it clarifies that formation and destruction result from the karma of sentient beings;
second, it clarifies the locations where the three calamities destroy the kalpa.
The three knowledges (*vidyā*) [reveal that] destruction, emptiness, formation,
and abiding constitute twenty kalpas, which is termed one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
Fourth, there are three [explanations] regarding the lifespan in the Brahma-world.
Regarding the statement that it is "due to the actions performed by sentient beings which can induce the karma for formation and destruction," this means that discursive thought (*vitarka*),
sustained thought (*vicāra*), guile (*śāṭhya*), and deceit (*māyā*) constitute the karma for the fire disaster.
Joy constitutes the karma for the calamity of water;
pleasure and the two types of equanimity constitute the karma for the calamity of wind.
These are produced by both wholesome and unwholesome karma within the desire realm.
The upper realms are exclusively wholesome.
Master Jing said:
"The momentum of the initial karma is still powerful."
The world is brought into being by the power of karma;
later, when the force of that karma declines,
it is caused to disintegrate and perish.
It is said that the karma of the age of decline constitutes the karma that brings about destruction;
therefore, the treatise states:
"Because there is the fire of vitarka and vicāra within, there is externally the calamity of fire and so forth."
The passage beginning with "By means of those external factors" and below serves as a general rebuttal to an objection.
The objection states:
The formation and destruction of the external vessel-world cease through the exhaustion of individual karmas;
the birth and death of internal sentient beings cease through the exhaustion of individual karmas.
The answer below states that because those external vessels are all completely dispersed and destroyed, they depend upon the karma of destruction.
Death within [the womb] consists merely of the exhaustion of the life-span and not of total disintegration; therefore, there is no separate karma of death.
The following explains why this is so: "For what reason?"
Because those external, non-sentient, coarse material forms abide in constant succession,
it is truly difficult for them to perish all at once;
therefore, their destruction is brought about by karma.
The consciousness of the internal body relies upon it;
as long as consciousness remains, life endures.
When karma is exhausted, life perishes, and [the body] naturally and spontaneously undergoes transformation and decay.
Furthermore, regarding "the karma that brings about the receptacle world and so forth," this refers to the karma capable of producing the external environment;
it necessarily draws forth [the duration of] one kalpa, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Because it is summoned by the collective karma of all sentient beings,
death within [the realm] does not occur in that manner;
for due to various karmas, the lifespan is indeterminate.
Each is induced by its own individual karma;
when that karma is exhausted and life has ended, one dies spontaneously.
Regarding the location of liberation, there are two [types].
First, it clarifies the locations destroyed by the three calamities;
second, it clarifies the location not destroyed by the calamities,
which is termed the "summit of calamity."
Next, the four kalpas are explained.
Each consists of twenty [sub-kalpas] to form one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
Among these, only the twenty sub-kalpas of the "abiding" period (*sthiti-kalpa*) involve both increase and decrease, and thus can be said to constitute twenty.
Since the three periods of formation, destruction, and emptiness neither increase nor decrease,
they should be understood according to the measure of the abiding eon (*sthiti-kalpa*) within the explanation of the lifespan.
The "Brahma who Benefits Before" refers to the second heaven,
the Brahma-purohita (Ministers of Brahmā),
because they provide benefit prior to the Great Brahma King.
There are nine kinds.
First is the calculation by days, months, and years.
The *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra) states:
Day and night, days and months, seasons, and years are counted by these.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* also states that there are two kinds of kalpas.
First, the number of days, months, and years;
second, the asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
and third, the kalpas of increase and decrease.
These are the calamities of famine, disease, and weapons.
A minor kalpa of the three calamities is called an intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa).
Twenty such intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa.
This is the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas.
Four periods of forty kalpas constitute one kalpa;
this is the lifespan of the Brahmapurohita devas.
Fifty or sixty kalpas constitute one kalpa;
this is the lifespan of Mahābrahmā.
Sixty or eighty kalpas constitute one kalpa.
This refers to the great kalpa of calamities.
Seven times seven [forty-nine] great [kalpas] constitute one kalpa;
this is the kalpa of the water disaster.
Eighty-seven cycles of water constitute one kalpa,
which is the kalpa of the wind disaster.
Ninety-three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas [constitute the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas].
According to the "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta) in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the Avataṃsaka-sūtra,
there are one hundred and twenty such numbers;
the one hundred and twentieth is named one asaṃkhyeya.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (She lun), there are thirty-three asaṃkhyeya kalpas:
the second [great] kalpa consists of twenty-one small kalpas,
and the third [great] kalpa consists of nine medium kalpas.
Because the first [great kalpa] is divided into three,
although this text exists,
it is not known how they accumulate to form the "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*).
If one examines the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, which cites the *Vimuktimārga-sūtra* as enumerating sixty [factors],
there are actually only fifty-two;
eight have been omitted.
The fifty-second is named asaṃkhyeya.
It likewise accumulates by tens;
it differs from the *Avataṃsaka*, which doubles the number for every value above ten thousand.
This refers to terms such as "myriad" (*wan*), "ten thousand" (*wan*), "hundred million" (*yi*), and so forth;
because the magnitudes differ, the numerical values they represent vary.
Furthermore, as found in texts such as the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) and the *Loutan jing*:
The Buddha taught the number of kalpas as being variously great or small according to the capacity of his listeners;
however, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites a sūtra stating that there is a city measuring ten thousand or a hundred yojanas filled to overflowing with mustard seeds.
Suppose there were a long-lived person who, after reaching one hundred years of age, took a single mustard seed away;
even when all the mustard seeds were exhausted, the kalpa would still not have ended.
This is explained at length.
Paramārtha says:
As the sūtra states, even if one were to remove a single mustard seed every hundred years until the entire heap of mustard seeds was exhausted, it would still not mark the end of the kalpa.
Because it is no longer called a "congregation," it is said that the congregation has ended;
yet because there is still a mustard seed remaining, the kalpa is not yet exhausted.
As for the statement that the lifespan of Mahābrahmā is sixty intermediate kalpas:
Traditionally, it has been handed down that the Brahmā King passes through only fifty-eight intermediate kalpas minus two intermediate kalpas. Why is this so?
During the kalpa of formation, the first distinct intermediate kalpa forms the receptacle world;
before the Brahmā King appears,
only nineteen kalpas have elapsed.
At the time of the kalpa of destruction, when the fires of a kalpa arise,
even the Brahmā King does not exist. Thus,
within one great kalpa of eighty intermediate kalpas, excluding the periods of total emptiness, there are twenty intermediate kalpas during which the Brahmā King exists.
At the times of formation and destruction, one kalpa each is excluded;
thus, the lifespan is actually fifty-eight kalpas.
To say that the lifespan is sixty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpas) combined into a single kalpa is [a conventional expression].
Judging by the general consensus of most sources,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The lifespan of Brahmā-rāja is fifty-eight kalpas."
According to the *Utpatti-sūtra*,
Brahmā King further completes sixty minor kalpas; it says:
When the world was first formed, the palaces of the three heavens of the First Dhyāna were first established,
while the palaces of the Desire Realm had not yet come into being.
At that time, Brahmā had already been born from a higher realm and was dwelling in the Brahma Palace.
Thereafter, the gods who dwell in the void of the desire realm and others are created;
thus, the formation eon (vivartakalpa) reaches its completion at twenty intermediate kalpas.
Subsequently, when the period of destruction arrives, it reaches the twentieth intermediate kalpa.
After the fire of the desire realm has already burned for a long time and Brahmā remains,
the force of the flames persists for a long duration until it nearly reaches the Brahma palace.
Only after the Brahmā King has departed does the kalpa of destruction proceed for another twenty kalpas; thus,
a total of sixty kalpas are fully traversed.
This is because it corresponds to the measure and stage at which the world, including fire and the other elements, first forms and perishes;
thus, the lifespan of Mahābrahmā is fixed at one kalpa.
Furthermore, the three heavens differ in their modes of rebirth through the three grades of cultivation.
The number of kalpas differs for this reason.
Question: According to this treatise, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and other texts, it is explained that nineteen kalpas are required to destroy the world of sentient beings.
Regarding the destruction of the receptacle world during the twentieth kalpa:
if one follows the *Lokasthāna-sūtra*, which states that ten kalpas are spent destroying the sentient world and ten kalpas are spent destroying the receptacle world,
how should this be reconciled?
The commentary states:
Their views and hearsays differ from one another,
making them difficult to reconcile and explain.
Furthermore,
another interpretation is that the sūtra states the world of sentient beings undergoes destruction for ten minor kalpas, from the destruction of the hells up to the destruction of the Brahma-world.
Before the Brahmā King has yet been born above,
because the Great Brahmā King is solitary and few in number, he is included within the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
This concerns the "many" and "few" discussed in the treatises.
This is stated as a general rule: nineteen kalpas for the destruction of the world of sentient beings, and one kalpa for the destruction of the physical world (bhājanaloka).
To specifically clarify the duration of the Bhadrakalpa is an explanation intended to supplement what was omitted.
Some say that this does not refer to the kalpa of water or fire,
but rather concerns the period before and after the appearance of the thousand Buddhas.
Because it spans a vast duration of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, such as those of fire and water,

the subsequent section clarifies that various phenomena can be found within it.
Regarding the initial passage:
Because it is destroyed by the calamity of wind,
the destruction by fire and water prior to its reformation is omitted and not mentioned.
According to the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World), it says:
In the midst of space, great heavy clouds arise, covering the trichiliocosm and pouring down a great torrential rain.
The drops are as large as chariot wheels,
and the mass of water increases until it reaches the Brahma-heaven, where there are four wind-circles.
Holding that mass of water so that it does not flow sideways is called first, "abiding" (sthiti),
and second, "firm abiding" (samsthiti).
The third is called Non-Compliance;
the fourth is called Firmness.
After the rain ceases, that mass of water recedes by itself for immeasurable *yojanas*.
At that time, great winds arose simultaneously from the four directions,
named Anabhirā; they blew upon this water,
churning it into a vast mass of foam.
The wind blows this foam and hurls it into the air,
where it first forms a Brahma palace adorned with the seven treasures;
that water then recedes and vanishes for immeasurable yojanas.
Again, he cast the water-foam to form the palaces of the Māra heavens;
next, he constructed those from Paranirmita-vaśavartin down to Yāma and Trāyastriṃśa,
forming them in successive order from the bottom upward.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"Just as after the destruction by fire at the end of a previous kalpa,
the three-thousandfold world-system below the First Dhyāna remains as a vast void for a long duration."
When the subsequent eon is about to begin,
a subtle wind arises gradually within the void of space.
Taking these as seeds,
he brought forth the seven treasures to construct the Brahma palaces,
as well as all the palaces belonging to the four heavens of the air-dwelling gods in the desire realm.
As for the statement "because their lifespan has ended," it means that the limited duration of life for those devas has expired.
As for "because their karma has ended," [it means that the propelling force of their past actions has been exhausted].
Because their lifespan in that heaven is not yet exhausted, yet their karmic force is spent;
because their merit is exhausted, they become addicted to the flavor of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the like, thereby relinquishing their life.
Although there are those born in the second and third dhyānas who possess [such qualities] from the outset.
Because there is no applied or sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and no further aspiration,
and because there is neither flattery nor deception, nor even the relationship between ruler and subject—
whereas these all exist in the first dhyāna— it is for this reason that Mahābrahmā gives rise to thoughts of aspiration.
According to the textual context, it is explained that as soon as the palaces are constructed, sentient beings immediately dwell within them;
they do not wait for the entire world-system to be fully formed before being distributed and settled.
As for the statement, "From this point onward, there are great wind-circles (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) and so forth," [it refers to the subsequent stages of formation].
Having constructed the celestial realms of empty space from above downward,
he next constructs the dwelling places of the five paths of existence below the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,
building them in successive order from the bottom upward.
First, the wind-circle is formed,
its extent equal to that of the trichiliocosm.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
The receptacle world is established as follows:
the wind-circle dwells at the very bottom;
its extent is immeasurable in width.
It is sixteen lakṣas thick.
Above that is the water wheel, eleven hundred million and twenty thousand [yojanas] deep;
its lower eight lakṣas are water.
The remainder congeals into gold.
This water and gold wheel has a diameter of twelve lakṣas and three thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas].
The circumference is three times this.
Master Bei said:
"To look up and see it spread all around."
This illustrates the mark of the rounded shoulders;
those spread out to the sides are like the base of a shallow bowl.
Master Ji said:
"Laying out [the lines] upward constitutes the lower part;
laying them out sideways constitutes the brick embankment."
It is like a grain basket that can withstand the splashing and pouring of rain and water from above,
yet is buffeted and struck by fierce winds from below.
Master Jing said:
"If the golden wheel does not descend to fill the lower layers,
the wind wheel will strike the water, giving rise to the principle of upward movement."
Pressing downward is called being struck and compressed by the wind-spiral;
this is the interpretation of Master Ki.
Now, in the Mahāyāna, the golden wheel is below.
The water wheel is on top;
this contradicts the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts.
Now, I shall further provide an explanation.
The water wheel is below and the gold wheel is above;
yet it is said that the upper [wheel] can withstand the pouring down of rain and so forth.
This means that above, it is struck by the pouring down of various rains from clouds that store the elements of the upper realms;
below, it is impelled by winds.
Although there is indeed a water wheel interspersed therein, [it is nevertheless unstable].
This is due to being successively impelled by the power of the winds.
Therefore, the subsequent text of this fascicle speaks in order of the wind-circle, the water-circle, and the earth-circle.
As for the seven golden mountains:
One yojana; this is translated as Mount Yugandhara (Holding the Pair),
because its summit has two ridges.
Second is Vinataka,
which is translated here as "Obstruction," because a deity dwells therein who obstructs wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
there is a divine spirit with a human body and an elephant's head who performs demonic deeds and can obstruct practitioners.
Because this mountain’s shape resembles the head of that spirit, it is named "Obstruction" (Zhangnan).
Third is Aśvakarṇa,
which means "Horse-Ear," so called because it resembles a horse's ear.
Fourth is Sudarśana.
"Su" has the meaning of "good," and "darśana" has the meaning of "seeing."
This is Mount Sudarśana (Good-to-See). It is so named because its mountain form is very beautiful to behold.
Fifth is Mount Khadiraka.
This is called "Wood for Carrying.
In the past, the asuras used this wood to carry Mount Sumeru;
because the mountain possessed this wood for carrying, it was named accordingly.
Sixth is Īṣādhāra,
which is translated here as "Holding the Axle," because its mountain peaks resemble an axle.
Seventh is Nimiṃdhara,
the name of a fish in the ocean;
this has no equivalent translation.
Because its mountain peaks resemble it, it is so named.
This differs from the sequence given in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) explains three kinds of iron mountains.
One should seek that text.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 172, states:
"Humans dwell in the four continents and also dwell in the eight intermediate islands (*antaradvīpa*)."
These eight intermediate continents are further accompanied by five hundred minor islands as their retinue; among them,
some are inhabited by humans, while others are inhabited by non-humans.
There may be those who claim that these are not celestial palaces;
as the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states:
Half a yojana beyond the eastern and western sides of Mount Sumeru, beneath the great ocean, lies the realm of the Asura King Vemacitra,
which is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
To the south of Mount Sumeru, at a distance of more than a thousand yojanas beyond the mountain, beneath the great ocean, is the dwelling place of the Asura King Vala-vikrama;
likewise, to the north of the mountain, at a distance of more than a thousand yojanas beyond the mountain, beneath the great ocean, is the dwelling place of the Asura King Rāhu.
Regarding the eight great *naraka* locations:
as for the various great *narakas*,
they are explained in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 172.
"Nara" has the meaning of "to create.
"Ka" has the meaning of "evil.
Thus, there are many meanings, such as that those who commit evil are born in that place.
Being alone, one may be in the open sky,
or in a vast wilderness,
or among the mountains, and so forth.
The cold hells are eight;
near the edges are the eight hot hells;
outside are the four types of groves.
This shall be explained in the fourth fascicle.
Animals have three dwelling places:
namely, on the earth, in the water, and in the air.
The great ocean is the source;
from this source they disperse to other places.
As for the abodes of the pretas:
Taking the abode of King Yama as its base,
it lies five hundred yojanas beneath Jambudvīpa;
there is a great kingdom there, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
From this original location, they disperse to other places.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are five hundred ghost cities to the southwest of Jambudvīpa.
They experience half suffering and half pleasure.
The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states:
"To the south of Jambudvīpa, between the two Iron Ring Mountains, lies the palace of King Yama."
It is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
and so forth, as extensively explained.
As for the term "one part":
Except for the fact that they dwell together with humans and devas,
Jambudvīpa is named after its tree;
Videha is translated here as "Superior Body."
Goddani is translated here as "Cattle-Trade" (Go-varta).
Kuru is translated here as "Superior Birth.
As for *yojana*:
The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:

"An atom (*paramāṇu*), a minute particle (*aṇu*), gold-dust, water-dust, rabbit-dust, sheep-dust, cow-dust, window-dust, a nit (*likṣā*), a louse (*yūka*), a barley-corn (*yava*), and a finger-joint (*aṅguli-parvan*)."
Each subsequent unit increases sevenfold.
Twenty-four finger-breadths constitute one cubit (*hasta*);
four cubits constitute the measure of a bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred *krośas*—
these eight *yojanas* amount to sixteen *li*.
As for the mention of "six thousand five hundred," [it refers to the distance].
This refers to the circumference.
As for the water of eight virtues:
first, it is sweet.
Second, coolness;
third, softness;
fourth, lightness.
Five are pure;
six are free from foul odors;
and seven do not harm the throat when drunk.
Eighth, drinking it does not harm the intestines.
As for the "Dragon Palace":
beneath the great ocean lies the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara.
It is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly square.
Furthermore, within the sea between Mount Sumeru and Mount Yugandhara,
there are the palaces of the two dragon kings, Nanda and Upananda.
It is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
the gods dwell within it, specifically designated as four tiers, each with its own level of residence.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings is situated upon Mount Yugandhara.
The Abhidharmakośa-kārikā says:
"Karoṭapāṇi, Mālādharas, Sadāmattas,
and the Mahārājika hosts."
They reside respectively on the four terraces and also dwell on the other seven mountains.
Master Jing says:
These various deities all belong to the celestial realm (*deva-gati*).
As for those called "Non-Heaven-Sided" (*Asura-pārśva*),
they are so named because they resemble the side of the asuras.
It is like Mount Vipula near Rājagṛha;
the Dragon King Susthita rides upon it,
and the tāla tree resembles the coconut palm.
The fruit is like the bowl.
On the side of the Great Golden Cliff is Lake Anavatapta.
As the verse in the Abhidharmakośa says:
To the north of these are nine Black Mountains;
within the Snowy and Fragrant Intoxication Mountains lies the Anavatapta Lake, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* later states it is on the summit of Mount Xiang. The commentary explains: [This discrepancy arises because...]
Regarding the measurements and the four precious mountains facing the continents, these differ from those in the *Abhidharmakośa* because they belong to different schools.
As for the path of the wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), it is stated that they merely circumambulate this continent;
such is the characteristic of a king who rules over the four continents.
It exists in other places as well,
for one travels through the air to those other locations; however,
it is only on this continent that there is a path of gold.
Regarding the Jambū tree,
the *Lokaprajñapti* states that beneath this tree there is Jāmbūnada gold.
The heap is twenty yojanas high.
Because this excellent gold was produced beneath a Jambū tree,
it is named after that tree.
All Jāmbūnada gold derives its name from this [tree].
The śālmali tree resembles the soapberry tree (sao-ke-shu),
but it does not exist here.
The egg-born birds dwell on the eastern side;
fanning the water with their wings,
they open up an area of two hundred yojanas to seize the egg-born nāgas.
When a bird born from a womb intends to eat a dragon born from an egg,
it likewise ascends the eastern branch;
the ritual application is as before.
When capturing a nāga born from a womb, one ascends the southern branch;
the waters part for four hundred yojanas,
yet one cannot capture nāgas of the other two modes of birth.
The ritual procedure for taking moisture-born birds, eggs, or womb-born nāgas is as previously described.
To take a moisture-born nāga, one ascends the western branch;
fanning the water, it opens up for eight hundred yojanas.
When taking on birth as an egg-born, womb-born, or moisture-born dragon through transformation, the ritual procedure is as before.
When taking on birth as a transformation-born dragon, one ascends the northern branch;
the waters open up for sixteen hundred yojanas.
As explained in detail in the *Lokotpatti-sūtra* and other texts,
at the beginning of the kalpa, humans were born through mental transformation (*manomaya-utpāda*),
with all their sense faculties (*indriya*) complete and without defect.
They travel by soaring through the air.
As for the "forest branches," their form resembles bracken ferns.
Husked rice, bran, and grain are the duties of the Office of Grain.
Some say that "bran" refers to clods of earth.
As for the "Director of Contracts":
"Sī" refers to the government office;
"qiè" refers to a formal agreement or limit;
"zé" refers to the official head.
Mahāsamata means "Great Equality of Intent.
It refers to one who is established as a leader because the assembly collectively shares an equal intention.
He is also called Kṣamāsaṃvṛti.
This refers to the "Field-Masters" (Kṣatriya).
Among all the Kṣatriya castes, this is the latter.
The Brāhmaṇas are here called the "Pure Conduct" caste.
Some say it is called "Inheritance of Tranquility" (Jìngyìn).
The Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna is named "Tranquility" (Jìng);
he claims, "I am the progeny of the essence of the Tranquil King."
Therefore, they are called "the offspring of tranquility.
Vaiśyas are said to "sit and gather seeds," meaning they sit and collect profits.
Śūdra means "one who plows the fields and sows.
Puguang (Bǔquè) quotes the *Abhidharmakośa* as saying:
"The path traversed by the sun across this continent has distinctions."
Therefore, the nights undergo both decrease and increase.
From the ninth day of the second half of the second month of the rainy season, the nights gradually increase;
from the ninth day of the second half of the fourth month of the cold season, the nights gradually decrease.
In the Western lands, the three seasons of heat, rain, and cold each last four months.
The sixteenth day of the first month is the beginning of the initial month of heat;
from the ninth day of the seventh month onward, the nights gradually lengthen.
From the ninth day of the first month onward, the night gradually decreases.
At the end of the period of increase and decrease, it is the opposite of this.
By how much does one day and night increase?
One *lava* increases;
when the day and night decrease, one *lava* also decreases.
The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) says:
The lifespan of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva) is five hundred years, and his descendants succeed one another;
they all dwell in and maintain their palaces there for the full duration of one kalpa,
until the sun begins its six-month northern course.
In a single day, it gradually moves six *krośas* toward the north,
never for a moment departing from the sun's path;
for six months, it travels southward.
Furthermore, within a single day, [the sun] gradually shifts six krośas toward the south;
during the course of the six months [of its southern path],
the lunar palace also travels that same distance over the course of fifteen days.
The details are as explained in the sutras.
Furthermore, according to the laws of the land of Han,
there are two intercalary months on the fifth day of the fifth month in the fifth year.
Regarding the swiftness of the moon's course:
on its southern and northern paths, it is swifter than the sun;
when it moves irregularly around the mountains, it is slower than the sun.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that the sun is cold when far from the distant mountains and hot when near them:
it is because the regions of the seven golden Mount Sumerus are hot due to proximity,
and cold due to distance.
Regarding the observation that the crescent moon appears when it is slightly inclined above [the horizon],
the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Because it is covered by its own shadow as it approaches the sun, the lunar disc appears incomplete."
Now it is not so. The moon itself becomes tilted and its own reflection obscures it, and thus its waning is seen.
Furthermore, there are devas and bodhisattvas who, with hands that are not those of the heavens, create obstructions to cause solar eclipses.
Regarding the statement that the reflections of fish, turtles, and so forth appear within the lunar disc,
other sūtras state that the reflection of the Jambū tree appears there as well.
The Tripiṭaka Master cites the *Prakṛtisūtra*, which says: "In the past,
when the three animals were practicing benevolence and righteousness together,
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wished to test their sincerity."
The hare gathered firewood and burned himself to provide an offering for the Emperor.
The Emperor marveled at his utmost sincerity; his remains were placed within the lunar disc to serve as a model for the world to emulate.
The *Tiandi jing* (Sutra of Heaven and Earth) states:
"In the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang guo*), the Bodhisattva Bao Yingsheng acts as the sun-city,
and the Bodhisattva Bao Jixiang acts as the moon-city," and so forth.
One *krośa* is equivalent to five hundred *dhanus*;
this measurement is based on the scale of the *chi* (foot) used during the Liang dynasty.
One bow (*dhanus*) is eight feet long;
five hundred bows are four hundred *zhang* long.
This is the resting place of the King.
This consists of two categories:
first, those created by great bodhisattvas;
second, those actually belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts among sentient beings.
Some say: Since this text states that it is due to the predominant karma of defiled experience, [the intermediate state is not included].
Since they are born within the *naraka* (hells),
it is known that they are subsumed under the destiny of hell (*narakagati*).
Other schools maintain that they reside within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) at a distance of five hundred *yojana*.
The meaning of "resting" is as explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
Regarding the wardens of hell, they are like those born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
As the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
The three hells of Avīci (Unrelenting), Pratāpana (Great Heat),
and Tapana (Heat) have no hell-wardens to guard them;
likewise for the three hells of Raurava (Great Wailing), Mahāraurava (Loud Wailing), and Saṃghāta (Crushing).
There are few wardens;

Regarding the fourth [verse] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are two interpretations.

using this passage and others as proof.
Second, it is said that this [state] relies on the stage of non-mastery, where for the most part the mind is sudden (*sāṃkathyika*) and lasts for only a single moment;
it is not produced from a mind that is a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*), nor from a mind of mastery, whether defiled or pure.
This is because it is conceptual (*vikalpaka*) and because it is projected by what preceded it.
Because it discriminates an object that has never been previously attained,
whereas [the former] arises because it is already familiar with an object previously attained.
Regarding the statement, "All that exists within the mental consciousness [arises] due to two kinds of causes," [it means as follows:]
If it is a resultant mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it arises from two causes;
if it is a resultant fivefold sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*), it arises solely from the fourth cause, being induced by a defiled or pure mental consciousness,
because it is devoid of conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*).
For this reason, the aforementioned treatise states that the five consciousnesses,

Because they take objects with which one is not familiar, these arise not through the power of attention (*manasikāra*), but are called "sudden, precipitate states of mind" (*ābhoga-citta*).
This is because they arise spontaneously without the application of attention.
The Tripitaka Master’s commentary states:

The *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) that arises abruptly (*sa-hasva*) takes as its object only that which was previously perceived in the past.
If it is the mental consciousness arising immediately after the five sensory consciousnesses— specifically the two types of mind consisting of investigation (*vitarka*) and determination (*vicāra*)—
it should be said to take as its object only the present objects of the same category as those perceived by the preceding five consciousnesses.
If this investigation were determined to arise from two minds, then it would arise by taking those [two] objects as its conditions.
Next, the Son of the Victor (Jinaputra) challenges the previous teacher, saying:
"Consider, for example, the minds of the Buddha’s and Bodhisattvas’ supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth."
A spontaneous and impulsive mind arises,
taking as its object either the present or the future;
yet, some claim that such a spontaneous and impulsive mind takes only the past as its object.
It does not take [them] as objects.
Therefore, the consciousness of spontaneous and sudden occurrence (*sahaja-āvega-citta*) universally takes the three periods of time and supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*) as its objects.
From the section "exclusively taking the past as its object" onwards...

This clarifies that after the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), two types of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—namely, that which investigates (*paryeṣaka*) and that which determines (*niścaya*)—arise taking as their objects the past objects previously perceived by the five consciousnesses.

This [passage] should be read as extending its textual connection to the following statement: "The mental consciousness arising immediately after the five consciousnesses takes only past objects as its domain, whether it be investigative or determining."
Because it pursues and takes as its object the objects of the five consciousnesses,
it arises taking only past objects as its object;
or at times, it takes an object that is of the same category as the objects of the five consciousnesses.
One should say only that it takes a present object as its condition.

the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), when sudden and impulsive, takes only a past object as its condition.
Because the objects of perception are not clearly discerned,

the mental consciousness should be said to take only present objects as its domain.
If this refers to the mental consciousness that simultaneously seeks and determines [objects] alongside the five consciousnesses:
It arises by taking as its object that which was previously perceived by those five consciousnesses.

To supplement this, the fourth interpretation is added:

If it takes as its object the aspect of the fundamental objective realm of the ālayavijñāna, it is said to take a past object;

Therefore, this is stated according to the principle of Vijñaptimātra.
If this mind arises, it arises by taking as its object a present realm that has been transformed by itself.

Consequently, by including the title "Universal" (*sarvatraga*), the characteristics of the specific-objective (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) factors—which pervade minds of all three moral natures—are also implied. The rest is omitted for brevity.

At that time, one then incorporates [the categories of] loss, gain, and so forth.

all that is perceived is real and is not a transformation produced by deluded cognition.
Through the repeated cultivation of this method of going and coming,
it manifests naturally according to its own nature,
for a duration of time corresponding to the extent of its momentum.

As the text states:
"That is to say, in all instances, up to those established as co-arising (sahabhū)."
The general summary indicates that the four conditions are established based on seeds.

The continuity of consciousness refers to the eighth consciousness;
it is that which continues all seeds.
Because it continues in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment;
as for "co-arising," it means that the seeds and the fundamental consciousness always function together.

not based on their active manifestation,

second, because it is the cause of all phenomena;
third, because it is not separate from consciousness.
If one speaks of seeds, one is speaking of the various consciousnesses.
Furthermore,
it is explained that within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), four characteristics are established upon all the seeds that function in continuous succession.
This means that the four characteristics are established based on all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Since all conditioned phenomena— whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)— necessarily arise together with their seeds,

Regarding the statement that there is "alteration after arising," this is intended to demonstrate that once something has arisen, it undergoes transformation and cannot endure for long, thereby inducing weary detachment.
Among the two types of alteration:
The first refers to the difference between preceding and succeeding moments within the same category of phenomena (*sabhāga-dharma*);
the latter refers to the difference between preceding and succeeding moments across different categories of phenomena (*visabhāga-dharma*).

third, from "Furthermore, by virtue of the seeds... onwards.
To distinguish this, it is pointed out that the four conditions are revealed through the mind.
Regarding the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), it refers to the seed;
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) serve as causal conditions for their own arising, and the actualizing perfuming (*vāsanā*) is likewise a causal condition in relation to the seed.
Furthermore, the preceding seed in relation to the subsequent seed is also a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
however, because it is abbreviated, only the manifest [condition] is mentioned.
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
This refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, where a preceding group opens the way for and guides a subsequent one.
The fourth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains this passage as follows:
"If these consciousnesses are such that, immediately following [a preceding moment], various consciousnesses necessarily arise..."
The general statement and the specific meaning do not contradict one another in their sense; however,
according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, matter (*rūpa*) is reckoned as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
However, although this refutes the notion that form is [inherently] a causal condition,
it is not the ultimate teaching.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra states, this is clarified by increasing the enumeration within the sixth section on the three natures.
Only the three types of wholesome [states] are established as lacking ultimate reality,
because they are said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
As for the wholesome that consists of desirable fruits:
Thus, the aforementioned acts of giving and so forth that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) can induce desirable results;
as for those that are wholesome and consist of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*),
these are the aforementioned acts of giving and so forth that are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Immeasurable wholesomeness" refers to the four immeasurables.
"Wholesomeness based on a support" refers to...
There is wholesome [action] with an object of reference that seeks the three realms of existence;
there is wholesome [action] without dependence that,
having no object of reference, aspires for nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, giving material things is called "virtue based on support" (sāśraya-kuśala);
performing virtue without material things is called "virtue not based on support" (anāśraya-kuśala).
As for that which is comprised of the root and its attendants, it is virtue.
The essence of cultivated wisdom is called the "root";
the five aggregates associated with it are called its "retinue.
Alternatively, it refers to the wholesome states subsumed under both the root and the preparatory concentrations.
Regarding the eight types of rebirth through merit:
first is the minor regional king of the desire realm;
second is his minister.
Adding the six heavens of the desire realm makes eight.
This differs from the ancient interpretation, which excludes the ministers of the desire realm and takes the universal monarch (cakravartin) as the ninth.
The immovable wholesome [karma] constitutes ten types;
that is to say, the wholesome karma of the form realm, the formless realm, and the untainted (anāsrava).
This refers to the sense of taking up the fruit of craving.
"Understanding phenomena" explains wholesome states with outflows;
"thoroughly knowing phenomena" explains wholesome states without outflows.
Skillful means regarding the Truth of the Path is called "thorough knowledge.
This refers both to the principle and to the phenomenon;
as for the phenomena and things, there is a general name that applies to all dharmas.
As for the meaning of its fruit,
it is the Truth of Cessation;
because it is secure, it is called "wholesome."
Regarding the four types of neutral [states]— those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and a portion of those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*)—
it is as stated in the *Fifty-five [Treatises]*:
"Those born of maturation are exclusively neutral."
Two or three [of these] can be obtained.
There are two kinds of the first;
therefore, the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts (*śailpasthānika*) pertain to all three natures (*tridhātu*).
In this text, only the defiled and the neutral are distinguished;
therefore, they are called "one part.
As for those crafts that are practiced solely for amusement, [they are not included].
To engage in crafts out of a defiled mind for the sake of amusement constitutes defilement; furthermore,
one may also engage in crafts for the sake of amusement while in a neutral state of mind.
The details are omitted here.
Regarding the statement that [certain actions] are not performed for the sake of livelihood and so forth, and are thus indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
according to reason, there are also cases where one engages in crafts and occupations with a defiled mind for the sake of livelihood.
There are also cases where one with a defiled mind, for the sake of surpassing others, practices the arts and crafts;
likewise, out of greed for fame and profit, one investigates and discriminates to initiate such artistic endeavors.
Here, for the sake of clarity, we cite only one aspect as a representative illustration by way of abbreviation.
The same applies to deportment (*īryāpatha*); transformations are of only two types: wholesome (*kuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*).
As stated in the *Fifty-five [Scrolls]*:
"One manifests transformations either to guide others or for the benefit of sentient beings."
One should know that this is wholesome.
If one wishes to test one's own playful exercise of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is termed neutral (*avyākṛta*);
this is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*).
If considered according to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they also pertain to the unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Regarding the "wisdom-eye" mentioned in the section on the seven additional bases (*adhikaraṇa*):
In reality, it is not form; however,
because its nature is similar to that of the eye,
it is discussed here.
However, these three eyes subsume the five eyes,
because the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) encompasses the dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus).
In various ancient sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes said that the wisdom-eye contemplates emptiness while the dharma-eye contemplates existence.
Some say that the Dharma-eye contemplates emptiness while the Wisdom-eye contemplates existence;
when these four eyes reach the stage of Buddhahood, they are collectively termed the Buddha-eye,
as stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
If the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) truly lacks the physical eye,
it is nonetheless said to possess the physical eye according to its manifestation as the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya);
as for the one who does not blink his eyes:
There are certain insects whose eyes never blink,
such as the eyes of cicadas and the like;
these are those with "defiled eyes."
One says it is the eye with outflows (*sāsrava*);
another says it is the eye with cataracts and so forth.
As for the "eye as the basis" (*adhiṣṭhāna-cakṣus*):
Thus, based on the original fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*),
the transformation eye (*nirmāṇacakṣus*) arises;
this is called the "eye of the basis" (*āśrayacakṣus*).
Alternatively, it is the locus that supports the faculty which is conventionally called "the eye"; therefore,
we now also establish this name as a designation.
That which has already attained the eye refers to the eyes of the past and present; that which has not yet attained the eye refers to the eyes of the future.
That which has been previously attained manifests again;
that which has not been previously attained [is newly acquired].
Because it is now newly attained,
the outflows (āsrava) that already existed in the ten stages must be abandoned;
for they are bound to their objects, and [the new attainment] abandons those bonds.
The Buddha-eye is untainted;
it should not be severed.
One who has already severed the [ordinary] eye—
Thus, the eye should have been severed previously;
because it has now been severed,
it is called "the already-severed eye."
It is not that one who has already severed the eye should sever it again; for it was not to be severed previously,
nor is it now something that has already been severed.
One's own eyes are called internal; the eyes of others are called external.
The desire realm is called coarse; the form realm is called subtle.
The fruit of unwholesome karma is called inferior.
The past and future are called "distant," while the present is called "near.
As for those who listen with discernment:
The two ears of the Universal Flesh Heaven are high-hearing ears;
they hear the sounds of virtuous speech.
One may also distinguish their superiority or inferiority based on the sense faculties.
Regarding "impure" and "non-impure":
the food consumed by the various devas and others is free from impurity.
That which is consumed by humans and others undergoes transformation into impurity;
furthermore, that which is universally pervasive and follows all the sense faculties consists of the aforementioned two types [of elements],
wherein the body faculty is omnipresent within the other four faculties.
I consider this to be the third [point].
Regarding the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
they are as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
First, there are sentient beings with form who differ in both body and perception,
such as humans and the gods of the desire realm, as well as those in the first dhyāna, excluding those at the beginning of a kalpa. Second,
there are those who differ in body but have a single perception.
It is like the Brahmakāyika devas at the beginning of a kalpa;
their three bodies are one in thought yet distinct.
It is also like those in the second dhyāna who, weary of fundamental joy, enter the equanimity of the preparatory stage (sāmantaka).
Having become weary of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and having abandoned it, one enters the fundamental [dhyāna] with joy (*prīti*).
There are four [factors]: body, thought, and perception are each single, as in the third dhyāna.
The first dhyāna is called "unity of perception" because its perceptions are defiled.
The second dhyāna is called "diversity of perception" because its two types of wholesome perceptions differ.
The third dhyāna is called "unity of perception" because its perceptions are karmic maturation.
The remaining three are the lower three formless realms (*ārūpya*).
In other locations where consciousness is destroyed, they are not called "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
As for "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-sparśa*):
Because the sixth [consciousness] simultaneously contacts [the object] and is capable of initiating speech,
and because it can take speech as its cognitive object,
it increases in both the sphere of sound and the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Contact that increases by way of designation is called "designation-contact" (adhivacana-saṃsparśa).
As for "impingement-contact" (pratigha-saṃsparśa),
it is contact associated with the five consciousnesses because their sense faculties are characterized by impingement.
That which is based on attachment refers to the desire realm;
that which is based on renunciation refers to the form realm, the formless realm, and the untainted.
"Savoring" refers to that which is with outflows (sāsrava);
"without savoring" refers to that which is without outflows (anāsrava).
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
"Relishing" refers to attachment to external objects;
"savoring" refers to attachment to the internal body;
"worldly" refers to conceptual discrimination.
The supramundane is called non-conceptual.
The nine [abodes] consist of the seven stations of consciousness, with the addition of the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are those with support and those without support, as well as the luminous form.
Master Bei said:
"The *Śāstra* provides three explanations.
One explanation states that the internal light within the solar disc is called 'having a basis' (*sāśraya*)."
That which emanates outside the wheel is called "without support.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the light of the ground is called "with support."
In the void, the light is named "Non-reliance" (Anāśrita).
Furthermore, it is explained that among humans, it is named "Reliance" (Sāśrita).
In the heavens, it is called "Independent," because it exists eternally.
As for the light of the correct and the incorrect:
This refers to the light of the waxing and waning moon and so forth.
"Matter that exists as an accumulation" refers to various material forms (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*).
The mutual dependence of the three wheels is called "establishment.
Structures such as houses are called "covering.
The seven types of appropriation are as described in the second fascicle.
Among the nine [bases], internal and external are not mentioned;
even if one's own or another's body were considered an external base, it would certainly be distinct from the sense faculties,
though in reality they are similar.
The *yaogǔ* (waist drum) refers to the small waist drum.
The *gānggǔ* (shoulder drum) refers to the large drum carried on horseback by officials of high rank.
The *dūtánggǔ* (large slender-waisted drum) is the large waist drum.
Regarding *stūluka* incense, it was formerly called *douloupo* incense;
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* calls it *kukura* incense.
As for camphor incense:
It is found in the Western Regions;
its fragrance is like clouds,
and its color is like ice and snow.
As for the *sukhī-melā* incense,
it is about the size of a sesame seed;
it is red in color and capable of being dyed to produce a deep hue— a substance not found in this land.
This is the supreme incense.
Regarding the three pungent aromatics:
in the Western lands, it is customary to combine the three flavors of black pepper (*marica*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and ginger (*śṛṅgavera*) to form pills.
When about to eat, one should first swallow this pill to eliminate what is unwholesome within the abdomen;
only then should one eat.
Regarding "fragrance for one finger-width," etc.:
Because its shape is like that of a finger-joint.
Regarding "the taste of healing":
this refers to tastes that eliminate the aforementioned ailments and imbalances.
Among the five types of contact, mosquitoes and gadflies constitute one;
among the six, that which is co-nascent is the fourth,
because it exists simultaneously with the body within the internal physical frame.
That which is to be remedied consists of the defilements and so forth;
that which remedies them consists of water and so forth.
The Dharma Master Xuan of Silla said:
Illness is that which is to be remedied;
medicine is that which remedies it.
This is distinguished within the dharma-dhātu.
First, the names and entities of the phenomena within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are enumerated in their entirety;
subsequently, the section on the expansion of categories is explained.
According to the Abhidharma, there are five kinds of form within the sphere of mental objects.
In this context, because it is presented in brief, only two types are mentioned.
Alternatively, regarding the two— namely, conventional and non-conventional phenomena—
the four types of form within the form-aggregate of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are conventional.
The substance of matter produced by mastery (*vaśitā*) is real.
Among the mental factors, the universal (*mahābhūmika*), the object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), and each of the five [wholesome] factors are invariably real.
Within the eleven [wholesome factors], only non-negligence (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) are conventional (*prajñapti*).
The other eight are substantial.

the other five are substantial.

according to the *Fifty-four [Treatises]*,

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*): these four are real.

vitarka and vicāra are definitely nominally existent (prajñaptisat).

namely, the conditioned and the unconditioned.

three natures are thus real.

space and so forth are indeterminate.

First, volition;

Master Jing says:
This refers to the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Master Ji says:

Seventh, cessation through deliberation;

This unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (asaṃjñisamāpatti/nirodhasamāpatti), being immovable,
is combined as the tenth;
thus it concludes that there are six hundred and sixty [unconditioned phenomena].
Within each of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the numbers increase one by one;
from one to ten, there are fifty-five instances for each,
and these two sets of fifty-five together total six hundred and sixty.
This is based on the possibility that there may be an increase in the number of factors, or it merely refers to a large number.
